h:
Every generation of rapture believers has been the last one.

William Miller said 1844. The Millerites sold their farms. Charles Taze Russell said 1914, then 1918. Hal Lindsey looked at the 1948 Israeli state and told a generation of Christians their grandchildren wouldn’t exist. Left Behind sold 65 million copies and the theology underneath it taught millions of parents that investing in the next century was a fool’s errand.

The date changes. The certainty doesn’t.

And somewhere in that repeating failure, nobody asks the obvious question: what does it do to a people when they believe they’re leaving?

You stop planting trees.

That’s not a metaphor. Ancient covenant people planted trees they would never eat from. They understood themselves as links in a chain that predated them and would outlast them.

“A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the sinner’s wealth is laid up for the righteous.” - Proverbs 13:22

That’s a covenantal instruction about time horizon. About how far your responsibility extends.

Rapture theology cuts the chain.

When every generation of believers is oriented toward exit, they stop building institutions, stop accumulating cultural weight, stop raising children with a 200 year vision. They raise children with a departure vision. Hold loosely. Don’t get too attached. This world isn’t our home.

That last line isn’t wrong in itself. But watch what it becomes when you attach an imminent exit to it. It becomes permission to abandon the ground.

Darby invented the dispensational rapture in the 1830s. It’s not ancient. It’s not apostolic. It entered the evangelical bloodstream through the Scofield Reference Bible, a study Bible that embedded the interpretive notes directly into the page, training readers to see the notes as commentary and absorb the theology as Scripture.

That’s not transmission. That’s inoculation.

The Ethiopian canon, which preserved Enoch, Jubilees, which kept the full angelological and generational cosmology Rome had reasons to delete, has no rapture. The Tewahedo tradition has no exit ramp before judgment. What it has is a people standing in their ground, covenant responsibilities intact, building toward the age to come rather than escaping it.

That’s not a minor liturgical difference. That’s a completely different anthropology.

Who benefits?

A church that thinks generationally builds schools. It builds legal institutions. It fights for land and language and the conditions under which children can flourish. It accumulates cultural soil and refuses to let it be stripped.

A church oriented toward departure does none of that. It builds conference centers and prophecy ministries and waits. It reads the newspaper looking for signs. It interprets every geopolitical catastrophe as confirmation that the exit is near, which means the catastrophe is almost welcome. Almost.

You get a Christianity that is cosmically passive at exactly the moments history demands it be most active.

Who benefits from that?

Not the children. Not the grandchildren who inherit a stripped field and no theology to explain why their inheritance was abandoned.

Not the communities who needed the church to fight for them and got prophecy charts instead.

At its core, rapture is narcissistic and self centered.

Every generation that believed the rapture was imminent also believed, without stating it plainly, that their moment was the climax of history. Not their grandparents moment. Not their grandchildren’s. Theirs. They are the terminal generation. The ones who get to skip death, who get to see the curtain come down, who are cosmically special in a way no prior generation was.

That’s not eschatology. That’s ego dressed in apocalyptic language.

The disciples asked Jesus when the end would come. He told them no one knows, not the angels, not the Son, only the Father. That’s Matthew 24:36. The instruction embedded in that ignorance is: keep building. Keep planting. Keep raising children with a long horizon because you don’t know how long the horizon is.

Rapture theology inverts that. It claims to know. And that claim to knowledge produces exactly the posture the ignorance was meant to prevent, the abandonment of generational responsibility because you think the generation ends with you.

The wound it leaves.

Children raised in rapture-saturated households often describe a peculiar anxiety, not the productive tension of living faithfully in a broken world, but a low grade dread about the future that was never theirs to resolve. They were told not to plan too far ahead. Told that geopolitical darkness was prophetic confirmation. Told that investing in the future was almost a failure of faith.

Some of them couldn’t finish what they started because why finish what’s about to be interrupted?

That’s not preparation. That’s the atrophied capacity for long term faithfulness, produced by a theology that made departure its horizon.

The ground was always here.

Scripture from Genesis to Revelation, if you read Revelation as completion rather than escape, is generational. God promises Abraham land and descendants and a future. The Mosaic covenant is full of language about sons and daughters, about memory passed down, about what happens to a people that forgets. Psalm 78 opens with an explicit call to tell the next generation. Because telling the next generation is itself the faithfulness. It’s the thing, regardless of timing.

There’s no exit ramp in that covenant logic. There’s death and resurrection and the renewal of all things. But the renewal includes the earth. It includes the ground. The inheritance isn’t escape from creation, it’s creation redeemed.

Rapture theology is Gnosticism in a suit. The body is temporary. The earth is disposable. What matters is the spiritual escape to another realm.

The 81-book canon does not breathe that air. Enoch sees the renewal of creation, not its disposal. The Meqabyan books fight for covenant faithfulness on this ground, in this history. The whole canonical vision is earthy, blood and seed and soil and the long slow work of generation after generation planting what they won’t harvest.

Your grandchildren need an inheritance, not a story about why you were waiting.

Pack your bags is not the gospel.

Build for your grandchildren’s grandchildren is.

“Thus said the Lord God of Israel concerning the captivity which I caused to be carried away from Jerusalem: Build houses, and inhabit them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruits thereof, and take for yourselves wives, and bear sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, and be multiplied, and be not diminished. And seek the peace of the land into which I have carried you captive, and you shall pray to the Lord for the people: for in its peace you shall have peace.” - Jeremiah 29:4-7
